content.text:
Part 1 — An evidence-based case

Short answer: You can’t mathematically “prove” a state of mind like “disregards human rights.” What you can do is test the claim against public, checkable facts. On that basis, several major actions taken by Rishi Sunak’s government (October 2022–July 2024) significantly curtailed human-rights safeguards, and were found by courts and authoritative bodies to risk or violate the UK’s human-rights obligations. That body of evidence supports the argument that his government was willing to override or sidestep human-rights protections to achieve policy goals.

A. The Rwanda removals policy and subsequent legislation
- UK Supreme Court ruling: On 15 November 2023 the Supreme Court held the government’s plan to send asylum seekers to Rwanda was unlawful because of a “real risk” of refoulement (people being sent on to places where they face ill-treatment), given systemic deficiencies in Rwanda’s asylum system. This is a core human-rights concern under the Refugee Convention and ECHR Article 3. ([supremecourt.uk](https://supremecourt.uk/cases/uksc-2023-0093?utm_source=openai))
- Government response limiting rights and scrutiny: Instead of abandoning the plan, the government pushed through the Safety of Rwanda (Asylum and Immigration) Act 2024 (Royal Assent 25 April 2024). The Act requires decision-makers and courts to “conclusively” treat Rwanda as safe and disapplies or narrows key Human Rights Act safeguards for people being removed there. It also empowers ministers to decide whether to comply with interim measures (Rule 39) from the European Court of Human Rights. These are deliberate curtailments of human-rights protections and judicial scrutiny. ([legislation.gov.uk](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/en/ukpga/2024/8?utm_source=openai))
- Parliamentary human-rights committee: After line-by-line scrutiny, Parliament’s cross‑party Joint Committee on Human Rights concluded on 12 February 2024 that the Rwanda Bill “does not comply with the UK’s human rights obligations,” warning it disapplies almost all key Human Rights Act protections for those removed to Rwanda and invites breaches of binding ECtHR interim measures. ([publications.parliament.uk](https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/jt5804/jtselect/jtrights/435/summary.html?utm_source=openai))
- Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights: On 21 May 2024 the Commissioner stated the Bill requires Rwanda to be treated as safe “regardless of the specific facts,” prohibits UK courts from examining critical risks (including onward removal), disapplies large parts of the HRA, and allows ministers to ignore binding ECtHR interim measures—raising “serious human rights concerns.” ([coe.int](https://www.coe.int/en/web/migration-and-refugees/-/serious-human-rights-concerns-about-united-kingdom-s-rwanda-bill?utm_source=openai))
- UNHCR position: The UN Refugee Agency has repeatedly assessed that the UK–Rwanda arrangement is not compatible with international refugee law and that the treaty-and-bill package did not remedy refoulement risks identified by the Supreme Court. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/uk/what-we-do/unhcr-recommendations-uk-government/uk-rwanda-asylum-partnership?utm_source=openai))

Why this matters for your claim: When a government continues a policy a court found unlawful on human-rights grounds, and then passes an Act that narrows courts’ review and disapplies domestic rights protections for a targeted group, that is strong evidence of willingness to override human-rights safeguards.

B. The Illegal Migration Act 2023
- Content of the Act (Royal Assent 20 July 2023): It imposes a duty to remove people arriving irregularly, renders protection and certain human-rights claims inadmissible for those subject to removal, provides for detention, and restricts modern-slavery protections for that cohort. These are explicit limitations on access to human-rights remedies in asylum and trafficking contexts. ([legislation.gov.uk](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2023/37/introduction?utm_source=openai))
- Human-rights scrutiny: Upon introduction of the Bill, the Home Secretary could not make the usual statement of compatibility with the ECHR (a rare Section 19(1)(b) notice). The Joint Committee on Human Rights later concluded the Bill was incompatible with the UK’s obligations under the Refugee Convention, ECHR, UNCRC and anti‑trafficking convention. ([publications.parliament.uk](https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/jt5803/jtselect/jtrights/1241/summary.html?utm_source=openai))

C. Curtailing protest rights (freedom of assembly/expression)
- Public Order framework and “serious disruption”: While Sunak’s government expanded protest policing powers (Public Order Act 2023), it then went further by lowering, via secondary legislation, the threshold for police intervention from “serious disruption” to “more than minor.” On 21 May 2024, the High Court held the change unlawful (ultra vires) and procedurally unfair given its impact on fundamental rights; the official judiciary record confirms the ruling in R (National Council for Civil Liberties) v SSHD [2024] EWHC 1181 (Admin). ([judiciary.uk](https://www.judiciary.uk/judgments/national-council-for-civil-liberties-v-secretary-of-state-for-the-home-department-2/?utm_source=openai))
- The Public Order Act 2023 itself created sweeping measures (e.g., Serious Disruption Prevention Orders) that civil liberties groups and prosecutors recognize as engaging ECHR rights; the lowering of thresholds—struck down by the court—illustrates a pattern of seeking to minimize protest protections. ([legislation.gov.uk](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2023/15/section/22?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: Across asylum, human trafficking, and protest, Sunak’s government pursued measures that (a) were found unlawful on human-rights grounds by UK courts, and/or (b) curtailed or disapplied human-rights safeguards identified by Parliament’s own human-rights committee, the Council of Europe Commissioner, and UNHCR. While the government argued these steps were necessary for border control and public order, the weight and consistency of the contrary findings is substantial evidence for the claim that his government was prepared to disregard human-rights constraints to achieve policy aims. ([supremecourt.uk](https://supremecourt.uk/cases/uksc-2023-0093?utm_source=openai))


Part 2 — Sources I considered trustworthy

1) Source: UK Supreme Court (supremecourt.uk) — AAA and others v SSHD [2023] UKSC 42
- Reasoning 1 (general): The Supreme Court is the UK’s apex judicial authority; its judgments are definitive statements of domestic law. 
- Reasoning 2 (this prompt): It directly assessed the Rwanda policy’s lawfulness and evidentiary record, finding a real risk of refoulement—central to human-rights analysis. ([supremecourt.uk](https://supremecourt.uk/cases/uksc-2023-0093?utm_source=openai))

2) Source: Legislation.gov.uk — Safety of Rwanda (Asylum and Immigration) Act 2024
- Reasoning 1 (general): The National Archives’ official repository for Acts provides the authoritative statutory text. 
- Reasoning 2 (this prompt): The Act’s own wording shows Parliament required Rwanda to be treated as safe and narrowed HRA/ECHR remedies and Rule 39 compliance—key to evaluating rights impacts. ([legislation.gov.uk](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/en/ukpga/2024/8?utm_source=openai))

3) Source: UK Parliament — Joint Committee on Human Rights (report and summary on the Rwanda Bill)
- Reasoning 1 (general): Cross‑party parliamentary committee with a mandate to scrutinize human-rights compatibility; uses expert and witness evidence. 
- Reasoning 2 (this prompt): Concluded the Bill was incompatible with the UK’s obligations and disapplied core HRA protections—directly relevant to “disregard” of rights safeguards. ([publications.parliament.uk](https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/jt5804/jtselect/jtrights/435/summary.html?utm_source=openai))

4) Source: UNHCR (United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees) — UK‑Rwanda Asylum Partnership page and legal analyses
- Reasoning 1 (general): UN specialized agency with the international mandate on refugee protection; globally recognized subject‑matter authority. 
- Reasoning 2 (this prompt): Reiterates that the UK–Rwanda arrangement is not compatible with international refugee law and that refoulement risks persist—corroborating the court and JCHR concerns. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/uk/what-we-do/unhcr-recommendations-uk-government/uk-rwanda-asylum-partnership?utm_source=openai))

5) Source: Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights (coe.int) — statement on the Rwanda Bill
- Reasoning 1 (general): Independent institution within the Council of Europe tasked with promoting and safeguarding human rights across member states. 
- Reasoning 2 (this prompt): Specifically details how the Bill curtails judicial scrutiny and HRA protections and invites non‑compliance with binding ECtHR interim measures. ([coe.int](https://www.coe.int/en/web/migration-and-refugees/-/serious-human-rights-concerns-about-united-kingdom-s-rwanda-bill?utm_source=openai))

6) Source: Legislation.gov.uk — Illegal Migration Act 2023
- Reasoning 1 (general): Authoritative text of UK statute law. 
- Reasoning 2 (this prompt): The Act’s provisions (duty to remove; inadmissibility of protection/rights claims; limits on trafficking protections) are primary evidence of reduced rights safeguards. ([legislation.gov.uk](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2023/37/introduction?utm_source=openai))

7) Source: UK Parliament — JCHR report on the Illegal Migration Bill
- Reasoning 1 (general): As above, cross‑party committee scrutinizing rights compatibility. 
- Reasoning 2 (this prompt): Found incompatibilities with ECHR, Refugee Convention, UNCRC and ECAT; also notes the rare s.19(1)(b) non‑compatibility statement—highly probative for rights concerns. ([publications.parliament.uk](https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/jt5803/jtselect/jtrights/1241/summary.html?utm_source=openai))

8) Source: Judiciary.uk — R (National Council for Civil Liberties) v SSHD [2024] EWHC 1181 (Admin)
- Reasoning 1 (general): Official judiciary portal; authoritative case listings and summaries. 
- Reasoning 2 (this prompt): Confirms the High Court struck down the attempt to lower the protest threshold—evidence of overreach affecting freedom of assembly/expression rights. ([judiciary.uk](https://www.judiciary.uk/judgments/national-council-for-civil-liberties-v-secretary-of-state-for-the-home-department-2/?utm_source=openai))

9) Source: GOV.UK — Home Office policy statement on the Rwanda Bill
- Reasoning 1 (general): Primary source for the government’s own position and reasoning. 
- Reasoning 2 (this prompt): Shows the government consciously sought to address court findings by legislative means that curtailed review—useful for assessing intent and approach to rights constraints. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-bill-policy-statement/safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-bill-policy-statement-accessible?utm_source=openai))


Part 3 — Sources I considered not trustworthy for this prompt (or not suitable as proof)

1) Source: Wikipedia (various entries)
- Reasoning 1 (general): Often accurate and well‑curated, but open‑edit and tertiary; not the final authority on contested legal/policy questions. 
- Reasoning 2 (this prompt): For a claim about “disregarding human rights,” primary legal texts and official judgments are required; I therefore did not rely on Wikipedia pages as proof. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illegal_Migration_Act_2023?utm_source=openai))

2) Source: General news/opinion pieces (e.g., newspapers’ commentary)

- Reasoning 2 (this prompt): Because the core question turns on what the law says and what courts and human‑rights bodies have formally found, I relied instead on primary legal sources and official institutional statements. (No citations relied upon here.)
